practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of logical protection?
A) Keeping a server in a locked room
B) Employing security guards to patrol the building
C) Using encryption to scramble stored data
D) Storing backup drives off-site
practice_questions.marks: C) Using encryption to scramble stored data [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two physical protection methods an organisation can use to keep its data safe.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct methods from: locks / biometrics / location of hardware / backup systems / security staff. Answers must clearly identify a physical method; vague answers such as "keeping data safe" score 0. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a firewall helps to protect an organisation's network from unauthorised access.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. "a firewall blocks unwanted traffic"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "a firewall examines data packets entering and leaving the network, comparing them against a set of rules, and blocks any traffic that does not meet those rules"). A further developed explanation or reference to hardware vs software firewalls scores 3 marks (e.g. add "this prevents hackers from establishing unauthorised connections to internal systems, even if the organisation's own devices have been compromised"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what an acceptable use policy is and give one example of a rule it might contain.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): an acceptable use policy (AUP) is a documented agreement between an organisation and its staff that sets out what employees are and are not permitted to do when using the organisation's ICT systems (2 marks for a clear, developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement that it is a set of rules for computer use).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, the AUP might state that staff must not install personal software on work computers, because unauthorised software could contain malware that compromises the whole network (2 marks for a specific, applied example with a reason; 1 mark for a vague example without explanation). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A small business stores customer payment details on a local server. Last month it suffered a ransomware attack that encrypted all its files and demanded a ransom. The business had no backup copies of its data and no disaster recovery plan.

Discuss the protection measures the business should put in place to prevent a similar incident and to recover more effectively in future.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two categories of protection with developed explanation and clear reference to the scenario. For example: anti-malware software would detect and block ransomware before it executes; encryption of the data at rest means that even if ransomware gains access, the data is already protected; a regular off-site backup strategy ensures that if files are encrypted by ransomware, a clean copy can be restored without paying the ransom; a disaster recovery plan ensures staff know exactly what steps to take, minimising downtime. Discussion notes that multiple layers are needed because no single measure is sufficient.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two measures identified and explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One or two measures identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A large hospital stores patient medical records digitally. It employs a team of IT security staff, uses biometric scanners on all server room doors, requires multi-factor authentication for all staff logins and enforces a strict acceptable use policy.

Evaluate the extent to which the hospital's current security measures are sufficient to protect patient data from all types of threat.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation acknowledging the strengths of the existing measures — biometrics prevent unauthorised physical entry to server rooms; multi-factor authentication makes remote account compromise very difficult; the AUP reduces risk of human error; security staff provide active monitoring. Counter-argument identifies gaps: no mention of encryption (data in transit or at rest could be intercepted), no mention of firewalls (network perimeter unprotected), no mention of a disaster recovery plan (if an incident does occur, recovery may be chaotic), and no mention of staff training (AUP alone does not guarantee staff understand current threats like phishing). Substantiated judgement — e.g. the hospital has strong physical and authentication controls but logical and policy gaps remain, particularly encryption and a formal recovery procedure, meaning the current measures are not fully sufficient.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two strengths and two weaknesses identified, with an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Points largely one-sided with limited evaluation.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

before.content_html:
Why Ethics and Law Matter in IT

Technology has transformed how we live, work and communicate — but it has also created new ways for individuals and organisations to cause harm, whether intentionally or accidentally. Ethics in IT means thinking carefully about the impact our choices have on other people, from sharing someone's photo without asking to building a system that stores private health records. Laws exist to enforce the most serious of these expectations, but our personal sense of right and wrong — our moral compass — matters just as much.

This lesson examines the key moral and ethical issues raised by modern IT, and then looks at the specific laws that protect computer users in the United Kingdom. Knowing these laws by name and date is essential — examiners expect you to name them correctly.

Moral and Ethical Issues

Privacy and Security

Privacy is one of the most contested issues in the digital age. Every time you use a website, app or search engine, data about you can be collected, stored and analysed. Some of this is harmless — a streaming service remembering your viewing history — but the same technology can be used to build detailed profiles of individuals without their knowledge or meaningful consent. The moral question is whether organisations have the right to gather and profit from this data, even when users technically agreed to lengthy terms and conditions that most people never read.

Security goes hand in hand with privacy. When companies collect large volumes of personal data, they take on a responsibility to protect it. Poor security practices — weak passwords, unencrypted databases, unpatched software — can lead to breaches that expose millions of people to identity theft, fraud and harassment.

Key Fact

Cookies are small text files stored on your device by websites. Multinational companies use them to track browsing behaviour across many sites, building detailed profiles of your interests, habits and purchasing patterns — often without users fully realising it.

Cookies and Data Collection by Multinational Companies

Large technology companies such as search engines and social media platforms generate enormous revenue by selling advertising based on user data. Cookies allow these companies to follow users across the web, recording which pages they visit, how long they stay and what they purchase. The ethical concern is that this tracking is often opaque — users consent to a broad privacy policy without understanding that their data may be sold to third parties, used to influence their political views or shared with government agencies.

The scale of data collection by multinational companies is staggering. A single large platform may hold data on billions of individuals. This creates a power imbalance: ordinary users have little control over how their information is used, while corporations and advertisers benefit commercially.

Monitoring of Individuals

Individuals can be monitored in many ways — employers checking staff emails, governments intercepting private communications, or apps tracking a phone's GPS location. Some monitoring is legitimate: parents using parental controls to protect young children, or employers monitoring company devices to prevent data leaks. However, covert or excessive monitoring raises serious ethical questions about trust, autonomy and human rights. The line between reasonable oversight and invasive surveillance is often unclear, and different people will draw it in different places.

Something can be legal yet still ethically questionable. An employer might have the legal right to read staff emails on company devices, but if employees are not told this is happening, many would consider it a breach of trust. Ethics is about what we ought to do, not just what we are allowed to do. Monitoring without transparency undermines personal dignity and can damage relationships between institutions and the individuals they serve.

Impact of Data Loss or Damage

When data is lost, corrupted or stolen, the consequences can be severe. At a personal level, someone whose bank details are exposed in a breach may face fraud, financial loss and months of stress resolving the problem. At an organisational level, a hospital losing patient records could delay treatment and put lives at risk. For businesses, a major breach can destroy customer trust overnight and result in large regulatory fines. Morally, this means everyone involved in storing or handling data — from software developers to system administrators — carries a responsibility to treat that data with care.

Key Fact

Data loss or damage can affect individuals through identity theft and financial harm, and organisations through regulatory fines, reputational damage and loss of customer trust. Under GDPR, serious breaches must be reported to the Information Commissioner's Office within 72 hours.

Laws That Protect Computer Users

The United Kingdom has a range of laws designed to protect individuals and ensure technology is used responsibly. You need to know the full name and year of each one.

General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) 2018

The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which came into force in 2018, is the main law governing how personal data must be handled. It gives individuals the right to access data held about them, correct inaccurate data and request deletion (the "right to be forgotten"). Organisations must have a clear lawful basis for processing personal data — for example, consent, a contractual obligation or a legitimate interest. GDPR applies to any organisation that processes the data of UK or EU citizens, regardless of where the organisation is based.

Data Protection Act (DPA) 1998

Before GDPR, the Data Protection Act 1998 was the primary data-protection law in the UK. It set out eight principles governing the use of personal data, including that data must be processed fairly and lawfully, held for specified purposes only, kept accurate and up to date, not retained longer than necessary, and kept secure. When GDPR was adopted in 2018, the Data Protection Act was updated (the Data Protection Act 2018 incorporated GDPR into UK law), but examination questions sometimes refer to the original 1998 Act, so you should be familiar with both.

Computer Misuse Act 1990

The Computer Misuse Act 1990 criminalises three main offences: unauthorised access to computer material (for example, guessing someone's password to read their emails), unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences (such as breaking into a company's server to steal financial data), and unauthorised modification of computer material (including installing malware or deleting files). This law is the primary weapon against hacking, ransomware attacks and other forms of cybercrime in the UK.

The three offences are: (1) unauthorised access to computer material — simply logging into a system without permission; (2) unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate further offences — breaking in with the aim of committing fraud or theft; (3) unauthorised modification of computer material — deliberately altering, deleting or corrupting data or programs, which includes deploying viruses or ransomware.

Communications Act 2003

The Communications Act 2003 covers the misuse of electronic communications networks. It makes it an offence to send grossly offensive, indecent, obscene or menacing messages using a public electronic communications network, which includes social media, messaging apps and email. This law is frequently used in cases involving cyberbullying, threatening messages and online harassment.

Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (RIPA)

The Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 governs how government agencies and law enforcement may lawfully intercept and monitor communications. It sets out strict rules about when surveillance, covert investigation and the interception of private messages are permitted, requiring appropriate authorisation. While it enables legitimate national security activity, it also acts as a safeguard against state overreach — agencies must follow defined processes rather than conducting unlimited surveillance.

Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988

The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protects intellectual property, including software, music, images and written content. It is illegal to copy, distribute or reproduce protected material without permission from the rights holder. In an IT context, this means that downloading pirated software, sharing copyrighted music files or reproducing images from the internet without a licence can all be criminal offences. Creators are automatically protected as soon as they produce original work — they do not need to register a copyright.

Health and Safety Legislation

Health and safety law applies to the physical use of computer equipment in the workplace. The Health and Safety (Display Screen Equipment) Regulations 1992 require employers to assess and reduce risks from the prolonged use of screens and keyboards. This includes providing adjustable chairs, adequate lighting, regular breaks and eye tests. Failure to follow these regulations can lead to conditions such as repetitive strain injury (RSI), eye strain and musculoskeletal problems. Employers have a legal duty to make workstations safe.

flashcard_questions.q: What does GDPR stand for and when did it come into force?
Name the law that was the main data-protection law before GDPR.
What year was the Computer Misuse Act passed?
Name one offence under the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
Which law covers sending grossly offensive messages over electronic networks?

flashcard_questions.a: Intellectual property — the original creative or inventive work of its creator.
flashcard_questions.q: What does the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protect?
Which law governs when government agencies may lawfully intercept communications?

flashcard_questions.a: Text files that track browsing; used to profile users without full consent.
flashcard_questions.q: What are cookies and why are they an ethical concern?
Name two possible consequences of a major data breach for an individual.

flashcard_questions.a: Repetitive strain injury and eye strain.
flashcard_questions.q: What health conditions can result from ignoring computer health and safety rules?
Under GDPR, how quickly must a serious data breach be reported to the ICO?

flashcard_questions.a: The right to have it corrected.
flashcard_questions.q: What right does GDPR give individuals regarding inaccurate personal data?

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Moral and ethical issues in IT include privacy, cookie-based surveillance, monitoring of individuals, and the serious consequences of data loss or damage.
  • The key laws protecting computer users are: GDPR 2018, Data Protection Act 1998, Computer Misuse Act 1990, Communications Act 2003, Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000, Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988, and Health and Safety legislation.
  • Always use the full name and correct year of a law in exam answers, and be ready to explain what each law covers with a real-world example.

before.content_html:
How ICT Has Changed the Way We Work

Advances in digital technology have transformed employment in two main ways: some jobs have disappeared while entirely new ones have been created. Changing employment patterns mean that roles in manufacturing, retail checkout, and telephone directories have shrunk dramatically as automation and digital systems have taken over. At the same time, demand for software developers, data analysts, cybersecurity specialists and social media managers has surged. Workers left behind by these shifts often need to undergo retraining to remain employable — government and employer-funded programmes help workers move into growing sectors like tech support, digital marketing and cloud computing.

ICT has also changed where and how people collaborate. Hot-desking is an arrangement where no employee has a fixed desk — workers book a space when they need one, reducing office costs and encouraging cross-team interaction. Teleworking (or homeworking) lets staff perform their duties from home, cutting commuting time and giving greater flexibility. This has been made possible by broadband internet, cloud storage and collaboration tools such as shared documents and instant messaging. Videoconferencing tools — including Zoom, Microsoft Teams and Google Meet — allow real-time face-to-face meetings between people in different cities or countries, reducing the need for expensive and time-consuming business travel.

Key Fact

Teleworking and videoconferencing reduce the need for daily commuting and long-haul business travel. Fewer car journeys and flights directly lower carbon dioxide emissions and ease congestion on road networks — a genuine environmental benefit of ICT adoption.

Effects on Transport and Traditional Media

The spread of ICT has reduced physical travel in multiple ways. Online shopping means consumers no longer need to visit a high street, lowering personal car use — though it has simultaneously increased delivery van traffic. Videoconferencing and virtual events have slashed the number of business flights taken each year. However, the growth of data centres and the manufacture of digital devices consume significant amounts of energy, partly offsetting these transport savings.

Traditional media — newspapers, magazines, free-to-air television and physical music stores — has been disrupted profoundly. Readers now consume news through websites, apps and social media feeds rather than buying a printed newspaper. Streaming services have replaced CD and DVD purchases. Many regional newspapers have closed because advertising revenue shifted to online platforms. While this makes information faster and cheaper to access, it has also reduced employment in printing, distribution and traditional journalism.

Drones, Green IT and E-Waste

Drones are unmanned aerial vehicles controlled digitally. They are used for parcel delivery, agricultural monitoring, search-and-rescue operations, film-making and infrastructure inspection. Commercially, drones can reach remote areas faster and more cheaply than road vehicles; however, they raise concerns about privacy, noise pollution, airspace regulation and collision risk with manned aircraft.

Green IT refers to practices and technologies designed to reduce the environmental impact of computing — for example, energy-efficient server hardware, renewable-powered data centres, device recycling programmes and power-saving settings on consumer hardware. In contrast, non-green IT involves high energy consumption, short product lifecycles, planned obsolescence and the disposal of working equipment simply to follow trends. The global shift towards cloud computing and AI services has dramatically increased energy demand from data centres, raising questions about whether ICT is truly becoming more sustainable.

Key Fact

E-waste (electronic waste) is one of the fastest-growing waste streams globally. Discarded phones, laptops and monitors often contain hazardous materials including lead, mercury and cadmium. Much e-waste from wealthy countries is illegally shipped to lower-income nations where it is processed in unsafe conditions, causing serious harm to local communities and ecosystems.

The manufacture of digital devices depends on rare-earth element mining. Elements such as neodymium, cobalt and lithium are essential for batteries, screens and circuit boards, but extracting them causes significant environmental damage — deforestation, water contamination, and soil degradation in mining regions. Mining is often concentrated in a small number of countries, creating geopolitical supply-chain risks and raising ethical concerns about labour conditions.

The Digital Divide, Social Media and Net Neutrality

Access to digital technology is not equal. The digital divide describes this inequality. Locally, elderly people, those on low incomes and people in rural areas may lack devices or fast broadband. Globally, large parts of sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and rural South America have limited or no internet connectivity. The digital divide reinforces existing inequalities — those without access are excluded from online education, e-commerce, telehealth and remote work opportunities. Solutions include government broadband investment, subsidised devices and community digital skills programmes.

Global production lines mean that the components inside a single smartphone may be designed in the USA, manufactured in Taiwan, assembled in China, and sold across Europe — a supply chain that depends entirely on ICT to coordinate, track and manage orders in real time. While this lowers costs and enables mass production, it also creates ethical issues around labour standards and increases carbon emissions from global freight.

Social media platforms have connected billions of people, enabling community building, political participation and rapid information sharing. However, they have also enabled cyberbullying — the deliberate use of digital platforms to harass, threaten or humiliate others — and the rapid spread of fake news, which is fabricated or deliberately misleading content designed to look like credible reporting. Both problems have been linked to increased anxiety, depression and social polarisation, particularly among young people.

Net neutrality is the principle that internet service providers should treat all online data equally — they should not slow down, block or charge more for access to specific websites or services. Supporters argue net neutrality is essential for a free and open internet; opponents argue that providers should be able to manage network traffic and charge heavy users more. Digital addiction — compulsive use of social media, gaming or streaming — is a growing mental health concern, with excessive screen time linked to sleep disruption, reduced concentration and lower self-esteem.

A passive digital footprint is data collected about you without your direct knowledge or active input — for example, websites logging your IP address, cookies tracking your browsing history, or a retailer storing your purchase patterns. An active digital footprint is created deliberately when you choose to share information online — posting on social media, writing a blog comment, completing an online form or uploading a photo. Most people have both types simultaneously, but many are unaware of the extent of their passive footprint, which can be bought and sold by data brokers without explicit consent.

Digital Footprint, Online Identity and Identity Theft

Every time you use the internet, you leave a trail of data behind you — this is your digital footprint. Posts on social media, likes, comments, photographs, search queries, online purchases, app usage and location data all contribute to a detailed picture of who you are, what you believe, how you spend your time and money, and who you know. This digital profile can be accessed by employers screening job candidates, universities verifying applicants, advertisers targeting content, and — in some cases — malicious individuals seeking to exploit it.

Your online identity is the impression of yourself you create through digital activity. A carefully managed online identity — a professional LinkedIn profile, a thoughtful social media presence, a portfolio website — can open doors to employment and networking. An unmanaged or negative online identity — offensive posts, complaints from former employers visible in public comments, photographs from social situations — can close those same doors. Once published, online content is extremely difficult to fully remove, and even deleted posts may have been screenshotted and reshared.

Identity theft occurs when a criminal obtains enough personal information about someone — name, address, date of birth, financial details or account credentials — to impersonate them, typically for financial fraud. Data harvested from social media posts, phishing emails, data breaches and weak passwords are all common pathways to identity theft. The consequences include damaged credit ratings, fraudulent loans or purchases in the victim's name, and significant distress and time spent recovering the situation.

Sharing inappropriate images online carries serious long-term risks. Once an image has been sent or posted, the sender loses control over it — it can be saved, forwarded and republished indefinitely. Images that seem harmless in a social context (for example, a photograph at a party) may damage future employment prospects or university applications if seen out of context. More seriously, the sharing of intimate or explicit images without consent is a criminal offence under current UK law. Young people can be targeted by people who use social media to build false trust before requesting or distributing images — a process known as grooming. The permanence of digital content means that the impact of sharing a harmful image can last for years after the original event.
